reasons to be skeptical
By Aaron Back
July 31, 2018 at 11:26 am ET

Procter and Gamble, like its competitors, is getting squeezed by weak pricing and
higher input costs. It has no clear way out.
The maker of Gillette razors, Tide detergent and many other household and personal-
care products is a bellwether for the consumer staples industry, which has been
struggling. The rise of e-commerce has made it easier for consumers to compare
prices between products and suppliers online. Retailers have responded by cutting

The company pointed to strong growth in its beauty segment, on the strength of
premium brands such as SK-II and Olay. Pricing in the beauty segment was also stable
from a year earlier. But prices fell in every other category, including fabric and baby
care.
Pricing in the grooming segment fell 3% from a year earlier, despite the fact that a big
reduction in razor prices was more than a year before, showing competition remains

intense. Online rival Harry’s, for instance, is now selling its razors in Walmart.
At the same time, higher input costs for paper and pulp, petrochemicals and freight
are pressuring the bottom line. The company’s net margin from continuing operations
fell to 11.5%, down from 13.7% a year earlier. That is the lowest quarterly margin in six
years, according to S&P Capital IQ.
P&G argues that it is turning a corner in pricing. Though many of the company’s
products are positioned at the high end of their categories, several price
“interventions” over the past year have gotten them within reasonable range of their
competitors, Chief Executive David Taylor said on a conference call.
The company also announced it will push through a 4% price increase for Pampers and
a 5% increase for Bounty paper towels and Charmin toilet paper in response to higher
raw material costs. But analysts were skeptical the company can make these increases
stick in such a competitive environment. In toothpaste, for example, P&G already had
to reverse a price increase initiated last year.
The company forecast an acceleration in organic sales growth for the current fiscal
year, which runs through June 2019, to 2% to 3%. This projection lacks credibility. The
company initially projected 2% to 3% organic sales growth in the fiscal year through
June 2018 yet delivered just 1%.
P&G shares are down 12% this year, and now trade at 18.2 times forward earnings,
compared with 19.7 times over the past five years, according to FactSet. Despite this,
the shares are no bargain until the company shows pricing and sales are firming up.
